first.text: Ah. Ah, no. No, no. Not yet. It's too soon for— you should be—
Forgive me. Brother Aldous Wren, of the Keepers of the Spire. Formerly. Currently of this bench.

choice.text: Mara says you can relight the Gull's Beacon.
I've seen the beacon. It wants a memory.
I'm ready for the rest of your story.
You said I'd make you talk. So talk.
Hold out your ember. "Look at it, Brother. Then tell me."

know_me.text: Know you? I— no. No. Everyone looks a bit familiar after the fourth cup.
He doesn't meet your eyes. His hand has drifted to cover the faded ember stitched on his sleeve.

spire.text: It went out. Fire does that. Even very old fire.

choice.text: You were there. You don't have to tell me yet.
Nine hundred years, and it just "went out"? Tell me the truth.

spire.text: You're patient with an old coward. I'm working up to it. Truly.
I've said what I'll say on that.

spire_gentle.text: …Thank you. I'll tell you. Not on this bench, not with this cup. But I will.
I can say this much sober: it did not go out by accident.

spire_pressed.text: The truth is a heavier thing than you'd think, Wakebearer. I dropped it once already.
He turns his shoulder to you and stares at the fog until you leave him be.

beacon.text: The Gull's Beacon. Yes. It can be lit. The ember isn't the hard part.
A beacon has to be fed. Not oil — memory. Something the fog left behind. A Remnant.
Whatever you feed it, the island keeps everything else… and loses that one thing for good.
That pebble in your pocket is humming loud enough to wake the Spire. It would do. Gods forgive whoever chooses.
Remnants wash up where the fog thins. That child with the collection of lost things — Pell? — may already hold one.
Go up to the headland. Look at it. Then decide whether you still want to.

after_beacon.text: So you've seen the cradle. Now you know why I'm on this bench.
People will tell you to burn whatever hurts least. There isn't one. There's only whichever you can live with having chosen.
And a Remnant needn't be found. Hold a loved thing in the grey long enough and the memory settles into it. We Keepers knew that trick. We knew it far too well.
Whatever you pick — come and tell me after. I owe you the rest of a story, and I'd like to pay it sober.

beacon_lit.text: I know. I felt it catch from this bench, like a hand on the back of my neck. Nine hundred midwinters, and it still knows how.
The lullaby. That child will sleep worse, and never know why. You chose something small that was everything to someone. They all are.
The founding knot. The village's beginning, for its future. A Keeper's choice — tidy, and cold. I'd have made it too. That's not praise.
Mara's brother. She gave him willingly; I saw her at the gate. That's a kind of courage I never had.
I promised you the rest of a story. The cork's in the bottle, for once. Sit, if you've the time.
There are things I should tell you. I'm not brave enough yet. Perhaps you'll make me.

spire_after.text: You've had all of it I can bear to give. The High Keeper put it out, and I held the door.
And something small and bright went down the stair past me. I think about that more than the rest.

confess_gentle.text: He sets the bottle down at the far end of the bench, out of reach, and looks at it the way a man looks at a dog he has told to stay.
I kept the east stair of the Hearthspire. Thirty-one years. Nobody climbs to the flame without a door-warden's say, and on the night of the Snuffing, I was the door.
It didn't gutter. It didn't starve. Fire that has burned nine hundred years doesn't forget how. It was put out — on purpose — by a hand that had every right to tend it.

confess_whose.text: The High Keeper's. Ours. The one of us who climbed highest and knelt closest.

choice.text: Why would the High Keeper do that?

confess_name.text: No. Names carry, in this fog, and that one is heavy enough to sink a boat. Ask me on Cindermoor, if we're ever both standing there.

confess_why.text: Why, I don't know. That's the truth, and it's the worst of it. I held the door and I didn't ask. Three months and a great deal of bad wine, and I still haven't asked.
But I'll tell you the part I never told anyone. Something came down the stair past me that night. Down, not up. A light — small and quick, cupped in someone's hands like a moth. I never saw the face.
His eyes go to your hand, and the ember in it, and away again.
When I first saw you, I said "too soon." The legends are very sure: the flame wakes someone when it fails. And it hadn't failed. It was put out. So what woke you, Wakebearer?

choice.text: Something that lit your beacon. That's enough for now.

confess_unknown.text: No. Nor do I. We'll be two people who don't know, then. There are worse fellowships.

confess_enough.text: Ha. Yes. It'll have to be, won't it.

confess_end.text: If you want more than an old man's word, the answers are where the fire was. The Hearthspire, on Cindermoor.
Nothing crosses to Cindermoor but the Tidewright ferry, and the ferry hasn't run since the Snuffing. Ferrymen won't sail into what they can't see.
With the Gull lit, they'll see Saltmarrow from the water again. Ask Mara when it's due. She knows the Tidewrights' ways better than I know my own order's.
He picks at the faded ember stitched on his sleeve until the threads give, and presses it into your palm.
Take it. I've no right to wear it. Some of my brothers might still open a door for that mark. Most would sooner shut one.

balk.text: Make me? Did I say that? I say a great many things.
You lit a beacon. Lovely. Go and look at what it cost them down at the harbor, and then come and tell me you still want a Keeper's secrets on top.
He tips the bottle up. It's already empty; he keeps it there anyway, until you step back.

confess_grudging.text: You open your hand. He looks at the ember a long time. The light of it moves in his wet eyes.
It didn't go out by accident. It was put out. By the High Keeper. And I was the door-warden on the stair that night, and I let it happen, and I ran.

choice.text: Why did the High Keeper do it?

grudging_why.text: That's all you'll have from me. I don't know why. I've spent three months making sure I don't.
If you want more than an old man's word, the answers are where the fire was. The Hearthspire, on Cindermoor.
Nothing crosses to Cindermoor but the Tidewright ferry, and the ferry hasn't run since the Snuffing. Ferrymen won't sail into what they can't see.
With the Gull lit, they'll see Saltmarrow from the water again. Ask Mara when it's due. She knows the Tidewrights' ways better than I know my own order's.
And Wakebearer — whatever you are. You came too soon. Remember I said so.

ferry.text: I heard. I'm not coming, before you ask. A Keeper on a Tidewright deck? They'd weigh me and find me light, and they'd be right.
Keep that sleeve out of sight till Cindermoor. It'll open a door or two there. Not before.
Thornwold had a beacon-keeper of ours, once. I'll not say the name. Names carry. But if someone in those woods looks at your ember like they've seen one before… be kind to them. Kinder than I'd be.
